strings.string: How the trail behind the second hand is coloured.
Off, the trail skips the five-second marks so it breaks around the numbers. On, it draws a dot there too and runs unbroken.
The faint dotted circle inside the hour numerals.
Random starfield, or the star pattern of a zodiac constellation.
Auto follows the current sun sign. Only used when the background is set to a zodiac constellation.

Colour of the hour and minute hands. Spectrum gives them no fixed colour: they ride the same hue as the second hand, turning through the wheel once a minute. The second hand itself is always the spectrum needle.

Cuts a hollow down the middle of the hour and minute hands, given as a percentage of the hand's width at the tip: 0 is solid, 50 leaves a clear border, 80 a hairline outline. The border keeps an even thickness, so the cut-out widens towards the centre. Too thin to show and the hand stays solid.

How many stars in the sky, 0-200, 0 for none. They gather along an arc across the dial like the Milky Way. Moonlight washes them out: the faintest show only near a new moon and fade as the moon fills, until a full moon leaves just the brightest.
Moves the hour numerals out to the second track, bigger and upright, in place of the 5-second numerals there.
What the hour positions show: numerals, numerals at 12/3/6/9 with bold ticks elsewhere, or bold ticks only at 12/3/6/9 with thin ticks elsewhere.

Every few hours a band of spectrum washes outward across the face, colouring the numbers, marks and stars as it passes. It runs for about 8 seconds, and fires on the first wrist raise after each slot.
The earliest hour the wave may fire, and the hour the interval counts from.
How often the wave repeats through the day. 24 runs it once a day, at the start hour.
Turn the moon copper during a lunar eclipse and show a corona during a solar one. Exact eclipse data is built in through 2045; after that the dates are calculated on the watch.

"Only when visible here" uses the last known GPS position to check the eclipsed body is above your horizon. It never needs a GPS fix, and falls back to showing every eclipse when no position is available. For solar eclipses this only confirms the sun is up, not that you are on the path of totality.
Built-in data covers 2025 to 2045 exactly. "Always calculate" uses the on-watch astronomy for every date instead, which is also how dates past 2045 are handled.
Reported by the watch. Anything typed here is overwritten.
Fire the wave at the top of every minute instead of on its schedule.
Render an eclipse regardless of the date, for checking how it looks.
Shifts only the moon and eclipse calculations, so the face keeps showing the real time. Leave at 0 for normal use.
Parks the hands at a set time, written as HHMMSS - 101035 is the classic 10:10:35 used for photographs. The date and the astronomy are unaffected. -1 shows the real time.
Overrides the GPS position for the eclipse visibility check. 999 means unset.
